passage: Ask people where they were when they heard of some great public shock, an assassination, a disaster broadcast live, the sudden death of a famous figure, and many will answer at once and in detail. They remember the room, who told them, what they were holding, the first thing they said. Such recollections have been called flashbulb memories, the name suggesting that a moment of intense feeling exposes the scene, as a flash exposes film, and fixes it for good. The people who hold them are rarely in doubt. Of all their memories, these seem the least likely to be wrong.

The difficulty is that when such memories have been checked, they have often turned out to be wrong in exactly the ways ordinary memories are. Researchers have questioned people within a day or two of a widely reported event and then again months or years later. The later accounts frequently differ from the earlier ones, sometimes in small particulars and sometimes wholesale: a person who first wrote that she heard the news from a colleague at work later describes, with complete assurance, watching it on television at home. Confronted with her own earlier account, she may concede that she wrote it while continuing to feel that her present memory is the true one.

What sets these memories apart, then, is not their accuracy but the confidence and vividness with which they are held; in these memories, conviction and correctness have come apart. One explanation is that the events are rehearsed endlessly. They are discussed with friends, revisited in anniversary broadcasts and retold until the story has a familiar shape. Each retelling is less a replay than a reconstruction, and the most recent reconstruction is the one that feels like the original. Emotion contributes too, but perhaps less to the record than to the sense of its importance: a moment that mattered seems as though it must have been remembered faithfully.

None of this means that strong feeling has no effect on memory. People rarely forget that the event happened, and there is reason to think that emotion sharpens memory for whatever is central to an experience while letting the periphery blur. The trouble is that the details we are proudest of recalling, the room, the messenger, the coffee cup, are precisely the peripheral ones. The practical lesson extends well beyond public events. Wherever memory is used as evidence, the vividness of a recollection and the certainty of the person reporting it are weaker guides to its truth than we are inclined to believe.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT:

passage: Public life has an elaborate culture of speaking and almost none of listening. Schools hold debating contests, organisations train their staff in presentation, and the history of rhetoric is largely a history of techniques for the person holding the floor. Listening, by contrast, is treated as what happens automatically when someone else is talking, a passive condition rather than an activity. Nobody is coached in it, and nobody wins a prize for it.

This neglect would matter less if listening were in fact passive. It is not. To follow an argument one disagrees with, a person has to hold its parts in mind long enough to see how they connect, resist the urge to compose a reply while the speaker is still in the middle of a sentence, and notice the difference between what was said and what one expected to hear. Each of these is effortful, and each can be done well or badly. Anyone who has watched a meeting in which three people answer a point that nobody made has seen what happens when it is done badly.

One objection is that a culture of listening would favour the patient over the right. If every view must be heard out in full, the argument runs, then bad ideas gain a hearing they have not earned, and those who are merely persistent will exhaust everyone else. There is something to this. Listening is not the same as agreeing, and a meeting that cannot end because everyone must be fully heard is not a model of deliberation. But the objection mistakes the purpose. Careful listening is valuable less because it is fair to the speaker than because it is useful to the listener: a person who has understood an opposing view can answer the strongest form of it, and can sometimes discover that the disagreement was smaller than it looked.

Nor is it obvious that listening must be slow. Much of the time lost in public argument is lost to misunderstanding, to replies aimed at positions no one holds and to corrections of those replies. A discussion in which each participant first restated the other's point before answering it might take longer at each step and less time overall. If that is so, the case for teaching listening is not a plea for patience but a practical one, and it is odd that institutions so devoted to efficient communication have left half of communication untaught.

options.A: Taking written notes so that each of the speaker's points can be checked against the evidence later.

passage: For several decades one research tradition in psychology has proceeded by a simple method. Set people a problem whose correct answer is fixed by logic or probability theory, record the ways in which their answers depart from it, and infer from the pattern of departures the shortcuts the mind must be using. The method has been extraordinarily productive. It has yielded a catalogue of systematic errors, and with it a picture of human judgement as a set of serviceable but crude rules of thumb that fail predictably whenever a problem is constructed to expose them. That picture has travelled well beyond psychology, into economics, law and medicine, where it is now invoked to justify the design of forms, defaults and warnings meant to protect people from their own shortcuts.

A rival tradition objects not to the findings but to the frame. A rule of thumb, it argues, can be judged only against the environment in which it is used, and the problems of the laboratory are often unlike the environments in which human judgement developed and in which it is mostly exercised. More provocatively, it points out that simple rules can outperform elaborate ones. When a decision must be made from a small sample in a noisy world, a model that weighs many cues carefully will fit the data at hand closely, including its accidents, and will then predict new cases worse than a rule that attends to one or two strong cues and ignores the rest. Ignoring information, which the first tradition tends to read as a symptom of limited capacity, can on this account be a source of accuracy.

The point is sound, and it is worth seeing why it does not abandon the idea of a norm. The advantage of the simple rule is itself a result of statistical theory: it accepts a little systematic error in exchange for a large reduction in sensitivity to noise, and in small, noisy samples that exchange is often a good one. To praise frugal heuristics on these grounds is not to reject normative standards but to replace one standard, agreement with a probabilistic calculation on a fully specified problem, with another, accuracy in predicting cases one has not yet seen. That second standard is arguably the one that matters for creatures who must act on incomplete information.

Where the rival tradition overreaches is in moving from what heuristics can do to what people actually do. To show that a rule performs well in some environments is not to show that people use it in those environments and abandon it in others. That further claim, that minds select their tools to suit the structure of the task, is an empirical hypothesis, and the evidence for it is uneven. People sometimes apply a rule where it serves them and sometimes carry it into settings where it misleads, and modern life supplies many settings, from the interpretation of medical test results to the assessment of financial risk, that resemble the laboratory more than the forest or the village market.

The disagreement, then, is narrower than its polemics suggest. Both traditions accept that judgement relies on shortcuts, and both, when pressed, accept that a shortcut can be good or bad depending on where it is used. What separates them is a question that neither has fully answered: how well people match their methods to their circumstances. Answering it requires studying environments as carefully as minds, which neither tradition, in its more confident moments, has been much inclined to do.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the rival tradition is best described as

passage: We tend to judge a portrait by asking whether it captures the person. A good portrait, on this view, reveals something of the sitter's inner life: a habit of mind, a private sorrow, the particular way one face differs from all others. Measured against this standard, many older portraits seem stiff and oddly impersonal. Rows of nobles stand in nearly identical poses, their faces composed into the same calm, their individuality apparently buried beneath velvet and armour. It is easy to conclude that their painters were trying to capture the person and largely failing.

That conclusion mistakes what such portraits were for. For much of the history of European portraiture, and of several other traditions, the purpose of a commissioned portrait was less to record a personality than to establish a position. The sitter appeared as a holder of office, an heir, a bride, the head of a house. Costume, setting and objects carried meanings that contemporaries could read: the chain of a civic office, a dog standing for fidelity, a column suggesting constancy, a distant estate glimpsed through a window. A portrait of this kind was closer to a document than to a confession. Its sameness was not a failure of observation but a deliberate placing of the individual within a recognisable type, since what the patron wished to have recorded was precisely the type he had come to occupy. A contemporary who knew the conventions could read an entire biography of rank in a single canvas, whereas a modern viewer expecting the revelation of a character finds only an inventory of possessions.

Likeness was not irrelevant. Families wanted to know what an absent bride looked like, and painters could be criticised for flattering too much or too little. But likeness served the larger purpose rather than defining it. A face had to be recognisable enough to attach the role to the right person, and beyond that the painter's task was to make the person fit the role. The expectation that a portrait should instead expose the sitter, catching him off guard or revealing what he might prefer to hide, belongs to a later and narrower moment in the genre's history. Where an older portrait does strike modern eyes as startlingly intimate, it is worth asking whether it was made for a public hall or for a private room, since the obligations of display weighed very differently in the two settings.

Several changes made that expectation possible. The growth of a buying public outside courts and great houses created sitters with no office to display. New ideas about the self encouraged the belief that a person's truth lay within rather than in his station. And when photography arrived in the nineteenth century, it soon took over much of the trade in cheap likenesses, leaving painters free, or obliged, to offer something a camera seemed unable to supply. The psychological portrait, in other words, is not the essence of the genre finally achieved but one of its historical forms.

To say this is not to claim that the older portraits had no inner life, or that modern ones are free of display. A shrewd painter could let a sitter's character show through the conventions, and a present-day portrait of a company chairman, with its carefully chosen office and posture, documents a position as surely as any court painting did. The point is only that we should judge a portrait by the question it was asked to answer. Faulting a court painter for failing to reveal a soul is like faulting a map for failing to be a landscape painting.

passage: Few findings from the psychology of decision-making have travelled as far as the idea that too much choice is bad for us. The claim has a satisfying shape. It flatters the suspicion that modern abundance has not made people happier, and it offers a tidy remedy: fewer options, simpler shelves, shorter menus. Retailers have trimmed product lines in its name, and essayists have used it to diagnose a whole culture of anxious shoppers frozen before walls of nearly identical goods. Its appeal, in short, owes at least as much to its moral resonance as to the strength of the evidence on which it was originally built.

The evidence, however, is less tidy than the slogan. A handful of striking early experiments suggested that people offered many options were less likely to choose at all, and less satisfied when they did. Later attempts to reproduce such effects produced a far more mixed picture: sometimes the effect appeared, sometimes it vanished, and sometimes larger assortments made people more likely to buy. A finding that reverses under slightly different conditions is not a law of human nature. It is a clue that the conditions themselves are doing the work.

What might those conditions be? The more careful research points to a few. Large sets seem to burden people when they lack settled preferences in the domain, when the options differ along many dimensions that are hard to compare, when no option is marked as a sensible default, and when the decision feels consequential enough to invite later regret. A wine enthusiast choosing among forty bottles is browsing; a novice choosing among forty pension funds is drowning. The number of options is the same. What differs is whether the chooser has a way of sorting them, and therefore whether the abundance in front of him registers as an opportunity or as an accumulation of possible mistakes for which he alone will be answerable.

This reframing matters because it changes the remedy. If abundance itself were the problem, the answer would be to cut. If the problem is the absence of structure, the answer is often to organise: to group options by the features people care about, to supply defaults that can be overridden, to let people narrow the field in stages. Cutting still has its place, particularly when most of the options are poor or nearly identical. But a policy of reduction applied everywhere would deprive the enthusiast of what she values in order to rescue the novice from a difficulty that better design could have removed.

passage: Philosophical discussions of ethics characteristically concentrate on the moment of decision. A situation is described, the available options are set out, and the question is which of them a good person would choose. This framing is natural for the purposes of argument, but it quietly assumes that the morally significant work begins only once the situation has been described. In ordinary life, nobody hands us the description. What we take the situation to be, which features stand out and which recede into the background, is settled largely by what we attend to, and that settling is accomplished before any choice is considered.

Consider a manager who prides herself on her fairness. When a request for leave arrives, she weighs it conscientiously against the requirements of the team, and she applies identical rules to everyone. Yet for months she has failed to notice that one reserved employee has grown withdrawn and anxious, while she registered immediately when a more assertive colleague appeared dissatisfied. Her decisions, examined individually, may be beyond reproach. The defect lies upstream, in a pattern of attention that has made some people's difficulties vivid to her and rendered others' invisible.

It may be objected that this demands too much of ordinary moral agents. Noticing is not something we do at will; we cannot be blamed for failing to perceive what never came to our notice, any more than for failing to hear a sound pitched too high for human ears. There is something genuinely correct in the objection. No single lapse of attention is a choice, and it would be unjust to treat it as though it were. But attention is not fixed in the way the range of hearing is. It is formed by what we have habitually looked for, by whom we have taken seriously, and by the stories we tell ourselves about the people around us, and these are things over which, across time, we have considerable influence.

The upshot is that moral improvement is frequently less a matter of resolving to choose better than of learning to see better. A person who wishes to be fair must ask not only whether her decisions follow sound principles but also whose circumstances reach her as calls for decision at all. This is slower and less dramatic work than heroic choice, and it rarely earns admiration, since what it changes is largely invisible from outside. It is nonetheless where a great deal of moral life actually takes place.

passage: Few arguments about words are made with more confidence than the appeal to origins. Someone uses 'decimate' to mean 'destroy most of', and a correspondent points out that the word comes from a Roman military punishment in which one soldier in ten was put to death, so that its proper sense is the loss of a tenth. Someone else describes an idea as 'nice' and is reminded that the word once meant 'foolish' or 'ignorant'. The assumption in each case is that a word's earliest meaning is its real one, and that later senses are errors which happen to have spread.

The assumption cannot be applied consistently, and nobody tries. If original meanings were binding, 'nice' would still be an insult, and so would a good many words now used without a second thought; the critic who insists on the Roman sense of 'decimate' does not, as a rule, insist on the earlier senses of the other words in his own sentence. Nor is there any principled place to stop. Most words have a history that runs back past the language in which they are now used, and the 'original' sense of any word is simply the earliest one of which we happen to have records. To treat that sense as authoritative is to give a vote to speakers who have been dead for centuries and to deny one to everyone now alive.

What a word means is settled, as far as anything settles it, by how the people who use it understand one another. This is not a counsel of indifference, for a shift in meaning can have a cost: if a word that once marked a fine distinction comes to be used loosely, the distinction may become harder to express, and a writer may reasonably prefer to keep it. But that is an argument about present usefulness, and it has to be made on those terms. It gains nothing from the fact that the stricter sense came first.

Etymology is not thereby made worthless. The history of a word can explain an odd spelling, reveal a forgotten link between two words that now look unrelated, or show how a community's way of life left its traces in the vocabulary, and it is one of the pleasures of knowing a language well; what it cannot do is serve as a court of appeal. To know where a word came from is to know something about the past of a language; it is not to know what the word must mean today.

passage: Why do so many religious and quasi-religious groups ask their members to do things that are difficult, uncomfortable or expensive? Long fasts, pre-dawn prayers, restrictive diets, distinctive dress that invites ridicule, vows that forgo income or marriage: from a narrowly economic point of view these look like pure loss. An influential answer, borrowed from the study of animal behaviour, is that the costs are the point. A signal that is cheap to send can be sent by anyone, and so tells an observer little. A signal that is costly to send, and costlier still for someone who does not mean it, is credible precisely because it is hard to fake.

Applied to ritual, the idea runs as follows. Groups that depend on mutual aid, sharing harvests, lending money or protecting one another, are vulnerable to people who take the benefits of membership without bearing its burdens. Demanding rituals screen such people out. Someone who is willing to rise before dawn for years, or to give up foods that everyone else enjoys, is unlikely to be only nominally attached, and the others can extend trust accordingly. The theory also explains a pattern that has often been remarked upon: groups that lower their demands in the hope of attracting members sometimes find that they lose them instead, as the value of belonging falls along with its cost.

This is a genuinely illuminating account, and it captures something that purely symbolic interpretations of ritual tend to miss: that rituals are not only statements of meaning but also transactions with consequences for who can rely on whom, and that their cost is part of how they work rather than an unfortunate by-product. But it is incomplete in at least three ways. First, it explains why a ritual should be costly, not why it should take the particular form it does. Any sufficiently burdensome act would serve as a signal, yet communities care intensely about the precise words, gestures and times of their observances, and would not accept a different hardship of equal cost as a substitute. Second, many of the most demanding practices are imposed on children long before they could choose them. A rite performed on an infant may say something about the commitment of the parents, but it cannot be a signal of the child's own.

The third gap is the most important. The signalling theory treats ritual as a message addressed to observers, as though the performer were already fully committed and merely needed to prove it. Yet people who undertake demanding practices commonly report that the practice changes them: that the fast or the vigil produces the conviction it was supposed to display. If that is so, cost does not only reveal commitment but helps to manufacture it. A person who has sacrificed much for a group has reasons to value it that did not exist before the sacrifice, and the observer who reads his devotion as a signal is reading something that the ritual itself helped to create.

None of these objections overturns the signalling account. They suggest instead that it describes one function among several, the one most visible to an outsider calculating whom to trust. A fuller theory would ask what ritual does to the people who perform it as well as what it tells the people who watch, and would treat the form of a rite as something that matters in its own right rather than as an arbitrary carrier of cost.

passage: Few natural experiments in linguistics are cited as often as the birth of a new sign language. Where deaf people who have had no shared language are brought together, at a newly founded school, say, or in a village where hereditary deafness is common, they do not remain without one for long. A system of signs takes shape among them, and within a few decades it has acquired the apparatus of a full language: consistent word order, ways of marking who did what to whom, devices for referring back to something already mentioned. The case is regularly offered as decisive evidence that the capacity for grammar is built into the human mind and needs only an occasion to express itself.

The evidence is real, but it supports a more interesting conclusion than the one usually drawn from it. A deaf child raised among hearing people who do not sign will typically invent gestures to communicate with her family, and these home signs show some structure of their own: distinct gestures for actions and for things, and a tendency to place them in a regular order. What they do not become, however long the child uses them, is a full language. The leap appears only where there are many signers, and it appears in stages. The first cohort, who created the system as adolescents or adults, typically use it with more variation and less regularity than the children who learn it from them; and it is those children, receiving a still untidy system and reproducing it more consistently than they found it, who drive it towards full grammatical form.

If grammar were simply waiting inside each mind for an occasion, the solitary home signer would have occasion enough. She has a lifetime of need, a willing family and an intact brain. What she lacks is other people who share her system and, above all, a younger generation to learn it from her. The emergence of a sign language thus looks less like the unveiling of a finished structure than like a process distributed across minds and generations, in which individual predispositions are amplified by repeated transmission until regularities that were faint in any single user become fixed in the community.

This is not to deny that the mind brings a great deal to the task. The speed of the process, a matter of decades rather than centuries, and the resemblance between the regularities that emerge and those found in long-established languages both point to strong biases in how children learn. But the case tells against the picture of language as an organ that grows in isolation, as surely as it tells against the picture of language as a mere convention on which people agree. A language turns out to need both a particular kind of learner and a particular kind of crowd.

passage: It is tempting to treat superstition as a residue of ignorance, a set of mistaken beliefs that education will eventually wash away. The difficulty with this view is that superstition does not distribute itself the way ignorance does. Highly trained surgeons, pilots, stage actors and professional athletes, people who know a great deal about the causal workings of their craft, are often among the most attached to private rituals: a particular pair of socks, a fixed sequence of gestures before a performance, a refusal to say certain words aloud. If superstition were merely a gap in knowledge, these would be the last people we would expect to keep it.

A more useful observation is that superstition gathers where two conditions meet: the outcome matters a great deal, and a significant part of it lies beyond the actor's control. Ethnographers have described fishing communities that use no protective magic when they work in a sheltered lagoon, where skill reliably brings a catch, yet surround voyages into the open sea with elaborate rites. The same people hold the same beliefs about the world; what changes is their exposure to chance. Examinations, sporting finals and opening nights share this structure. Preparation counts, but on the day itself something unaccountable remains, and the ritual fills the space that preparation cannot reach.

What the ritual supplies, on this account, is not a causal lever over the outcome but a way of acting when no further useful action is available. Anxiety in the face of uncertainty tends to seek an outlet, and an outlet that is fixed, brief and familiar is better than one that is improvised, such as a last-minute change to a plan that was sound. A tennis player who bounces the ball exactly the same number of times before every serve is not, in any serious sense, trying to bend the laws of physics. She is marking a boundary between deliberation and execution, and the routine protects the execution from second thoughts.

None of this makes superstition harmless. The same disposition that steadies a performer can lead a patient to choose a charm over a treatment that works, or a trader to mistake a lucky streak for a method. The line falls roughly where the ritual stops occupying the residue of chance and begins to displace action that would genuinely improve the odds. Understood this way, superstition is neither a quaint error to be laughed at nor a hidden wisdom to be celebrated, but a predictable human response to exposure that deserves to be judged by what it crowds out.

passage: Defenders of live theatre, when pressed to explain why anyone should purchase an expensive ticket to see what could be watched more cheaply and comfortably on a screen, usually appeal to presence. The actors are there, in the same room, breathing the same air; on screen they are only images. The answer is sincere, but considered as an argument it is considerably weaker than it sounds. A great many things are physically present to us without being valuable for that reason, and a lecture delivered in person is not obviously better than the same lecture recorded. If presence were all that distinguished the stage, the case for theatre would rest on something close to a superstition about physical proximity.

A more promising answer begins from what presence makes possible. A filmed performance is complete before any viewer encounters it; nothing the viewer does, however attentive or distracted, can reach back and alter it. A stage performance is still being made while the audience watches, and the audience is among the conditions under which it is made. Actors in a comedy learn to hold a line until the laughter at the previous one has crested and begun to fall, and the length of that pause differs from night to night because the laughter does. In a tense scene, a silence of a particular quality in the house tells the performers that they have the room, and they may let a moment stretch further than they would before a restless audience. These adjustments are individually small, but cumulatively they mean that a stage performance can be, in part, a response to the particular people assembled to witness it.

The audience, moreover, is conscious of this reciprocity. Spectators in a theatre are aware that they can be heard and, in an intimate space, seen; they are also aware of one another, and a laugh that spreads along a row, or fails to, shapes what each person feels. The experience is less that of watching an object than of taking part, in a minor and mostly silent way, in an event whose outcome is not wholly settled. That is why a performance can fail in the theatre in a way that a film cannot: not through a flaw in its making, which a film may also have, but through a breakdown between stage and house.

It may be objected that this account flatters most actual theatre, which is rarely so delicately attuned to its spectators. Many productions are drilled to such precision that they vary little from night to night, and in a large commercial house the performers can barely see past the first rows. That is true, and it calls for a qualification rather than a retraction. The responsiveness described here is a capacity of the live form, not a guarantee; a production can choose to use it or to suppress it, and one that suppresses it entirely has given up the main thing that the stage offers and the screen does not. Film, meanwhile, has resources of its own, the close-up and the edit among them, and nothing here implies that it is a lesser art.

The case for live theatre, then, is not that the actors are physically near but that the performance and its audience remain capable of affecting one another. It follows, perhaps uncomfortably for some institutions, that the strongest argument for theatre is simultaneously a demand upon it. A theatre that wishes to justify its prices by appealing to liveness owes its audience a performance in which liveness actually does some work.

passage: Many historians regard the question 'what if?' as a parlour game, an amusement for the armchair strategist that has no place in serious scholarship. The past, they say, happened only one way, and the historian's task is to explain that way, not to speculate about others for which no evidence could ever exist. The objection has the appeal of modesty, but it rests on a misunderstanding of what historians already do. To say that a harvest failure caused a revolt is to say, at the very least, that without the failure the revolt would not have occurred when and as it did, or would have been less likely. Every causal claim carries such a counterfactual inside it, and the historian who refuses to examine counterfactuals has not avoided them; he has merely declined to inspect the ones he is already using.

The real question, then, is not whether to reason counterfactually but how to do it with discipline. Two constraints seem essential. The first is that the altered antecedent should be minimal and plausible in its own time: the most useful alternatives are those that people at the moment actually contemplated, such as a decision that was debated and narrowly taken, rather than those that require rewriting the character of a ruler or the technology of an age. The second is that the horizon of consequences should be short. Each step away from the altered moment multiplies the contingencies in play, and within a few years the alternative world becomes as indeterminate as the future, which is why the popular genre of imagining a whole century transformed by one changed battle is closer to fiction than to history.

A more searching objection holds that even a disciplined counterfactual smuggles in assumptions about how societies behave, about which pressures are strong and which choices are free, that cannot themselves be tested. This is true, but it is not peculiar to counterfactuals. The ordinary causal explanation rests on exactly the same assumptions; it simply leaves them unstated. What the explicit counterfactual offers is not freedom from such assumptions but exposure of them, so that a reader can see what the explanation depends on and dispute it.

Used this way, the counterfactual is less a tool for discovering what would have happened than a tool for testing what is claimed to have been bound to happen. Historians and politicians alike are fond of declaring outcomes inevitable. To show that a serious alternative was open, contemplated and within reach at the time is enough to defeat that claim, even when nothing reliable can be said about where the alternative would have led.

passage: Arguments about public statues tend to be conducted as if there were only two positions. On one side are those who say that the statue of a figure now held in disrepute should come down, because a city ought not to go on honouring what it has come to find shameful. On the other are those who say that removing it 'erases history', and that a mature society learns from its past instead of hiding it. The quarrel is loud, and it is often bitter, because each side suspects the other of bad faith: of wishing to rewrite the past, or of wishing to keep its injustices on a pedestal. Each side assumes it knows what a statue is. Neither, I think, quite does.

A statue is not a history lesson. It records almost nothing about the life of its subject: a name, a pair of dates, perhaps a line of praise. What it records very precisely is a decision, taken at a particular moment by particular people, to honour that subject in that place. Many of the statues now in dispute were raised long after the events they commemorate, often by committees with purposes of their own, such as asserting the standing of a group or a cause at a time when that standing was being questioned. A statue is therefore better evidence about the people who raised it than about the person it depicts.

Seen in this light, the charge of erasing history loses much of its force. Taking a statue down does not alter what happened, and the books, records and family memories that tell its subject's story remain where they were. What removal changes is a present act of honour, and every generation is entitled to reconsider whom it honours. Yet the other camp should not feel wholly vindicated. A statue that is quietly carted away also removes evidence of what an earlier generation chose to celebrate, and that evidence can be uncomfortable in useful ways, reminding a city that the values it now rejects were once publicly and confidently held by respectable people.

The popular compromise of leaving the statue in place and adding an explanatory plaque is often presented as the neutral option. It is not. A plaque is also an editorial act: someone must decide what it says, how long it is and whose judgement it expresses, and a few lines of small print beneath a towering bronze figure rarely win the argument with it. Moving a statue to a museum, where the date and purpose of its making can be displayed alongside it, may come closer to keeping the evidence without continuing the honour. Whatever a community decides, it should at least be clear that it is deciding how to honour, not whether to remember.

passage: The story is told in so many introductory textbooks that it has come to seem like common sense. Once upon a time, it runs, people traded goods directly: a farmer with grain who wanted shoes had to find a shoemaker who happened to want grain. Because such a coincidence was rare, someone eventually hit on the idea of a commodity everyone would accept, such as shells, salt or metal, and money was born. Credit and debt, in this account, come last, a refinement that becomes possible only once coins are available to measure what is owed.

The difficulty is that the story describes a world no one has found. Anthropologists who went looking for economies in which neighbours regularly exchanged goods by barter have, on the whole, come back empty-handed. What they found instead, in village after village, was something closer to running accounts. A woman who needs a pot from her neighbour simply takes it, and both understand that something will be owed; the debt may be repaid in grain at harvest, in labour at a wedding, or never precisely at all. Among people who expect to keep living beside one another, the problem of the double coincidence of wants scarcely arises, because no one needs the exchange to be completed on the spot.

Barter does occur, but in revealing places. It appears between strangers who do not expect to meet again, between groups who distrust each other, and among people who were once used to money and have been cut off from it, such as prisoners trading cigarettes or townspeople whose currency has collapsed. In each case barter is a response to the absence of trust, not the primitive condition out of which trust and credit later grew.

Defenders of the textbook story sometimes reply that it was never intended as history. It is, they say, a thought experiment showing why a medium of exchange is useful, and its value does not depend on whether any society actually passed through a barter stage. This is a fair point as far as it goes. But the thought experiment is not idle. By placing money first and debt last, it teaches us to see money as a neutral token that merely smooths trade between independent individuals, rather than as a way of recording obligations between people already bound to one another. If the record points the other way, the more natural conclusion is that money began as a method of keeping score.

passage: Few historical lessons are repeated as confidently as the one drawn from the settlement that followed the First World War. A harsh peace, the lesson runs, breeds resentment, and resentment breeds the next war; a generous peace, by contrast, turns yesterday's enemy into tomorrow's partner. The lesson is attractive because it joins morality to prudence. It tells victors that magnanimity is not only noble but wise, and that they can secure the future simply by being kind. It also offers a single, memorable explanation for one of the great catastrophes of the last century, and explanations of that kind are hard to dislodge once they have settled into textbooks and speeches.

The trouble is that the record does not sort so neatly. Some severe settlements have held for generations, because the defeated party was too weak to overturn them and the victors remained willing to enforce their terms. Some lenient ones have failed, because the loser read leniency as a sign that it had not really been beaten and that a second attempt might succeed. What such cases suggest is that severity and generosity are the wrong variables to watch. A settlement lasts when its terms match the actual balance of strength, and when the powers that wrote it remain prepared to uphold it.

By this measure, the worst settlement is not the harshest but the one that combines harsh terms with a weak will to enforce them. Such a peace gives the defeated every reason to resent the order and no reason to fear challenging it. Its demands are heavy enough to humiliate, yet the victors, tired of war and divided among themselves, let them be evaded piece by piece, until the settlement has lost both its authority and its power to deter. Much of the interwar story can be told in this way, as a failure less of severity than of follow-through.

This is not an argument for cruelty dressed up as realism. Generosity has a real role, but it works best after the defeat has been made unmistakable, when it can be read as the confidence of a winner rather than the hesitation of a power unsure of its victory. Offering a defeated state a path back into the community of nations, through trade, membership of institutions and the eventual lifting of restrictions, gives it a stake in the order that no amount of punishment can create. The point is only that kindness must rest on a settlement that is clear about who won and is backed by someone willing to say so.

passage: Arguments about free will customarily proceed in a fixed order. First we are asked to settle a question about the world: whether every event, including every human choice, is determined by antecedent causes. Only then, it is assumed, can we know whether anyone is genuinely responsible for anything, and therefore whether blame and praise are ever deserved. If the causal question is answered one way, our practices of holding one another responsible are vindicated; if it is answered the other way, those practices are exposed as resting on an illusion, and intellectual honesty requires us to abandon them.

An influential alternative reverses this order. It begins not with metaphysics but with the attitudes we actually adopt toward one another: resentment when we are injured through someone's indifference, gratitude when we are helped through their goodwill, indignation on behalf of others who have been mistreated. These attitudes, the alternative maintains, are not conclusions derived from a theory about causation. They are constitutive of what it is to live among persons rather than merely alongside objects, and to suppose that a philosophical thesis could oblige us to relinquish them is to misunderstand both the thesis and ourselves. We do suspend them in particular cases: when someone acted under duress, or did not know what he was doing, or is a young child. But these suspensions are made within the practice, for reasons the practice itself recognises, and none of them amounts to a general verdict on human agency.

There is much to admire in this reversal. It explains why the free will debate so often seems unreal to people outside it, who continue resenting and forgiving whatever the latest argument concludes, and it rightly insists that responsibility is something we do together rather than a concealed property awaiting detection. Responsibility, on this picture, resembles a language more than a fact of nature: it is sustained by shared expectations, and its rules are learned by taking part in it. The reversal also shows why the most sweeping sceptical arguments overreach: from the bare claim that choices have causes, nothing follows about whether a particular person was acting under duress, or in ignorance, or as a child acts.

Yet the reversal is sometimes taken to establish more than it can. If the practice is answerable only to itself, it may seem immune to criticism, and its present configuration may seem beyond question. The history of the practice tells against such complacency. Over time, many societies have come to regard certain compulsions, illnesses and conditions of upbringing as diminishing responsibility where they were formerly treated as plain wickedness. These revisions were not imposed by metaphysics; they arose when people learned more about how particular capacities can fail, and then applied excusing principles the practice already contained to cases it had previously judged harshly.

This is where the sciences of the mind may matter after all, though not in the way the traditional debate supposed. No general thesis about determinism will tell us whether blame is ever deserved. But detailed findings about how self-control develops, or how it is impaired, can reveal that the conditions our practice already counts as excusing are more common, or less conspicuous, than we had assumed. A discovery that some apparent callousness is in fact an inability to register the distress of others, for instance, would not refute the practice; it would require the practice to be consistent with itself. The practice of holding responsible is neither a fixed point beyond inquiry nor a conclusion awaiting metaphysical proof. It is a body of standards that can be held to its own commitments, and inquiry into the mind is one of the ways in which that is done.

passage: It is widely believed that there is a window for learning languages, open in early childhood and closed by adolescence, after which a new language can be studied but never truly acquired. The belief has some foundation. On average, people who begin a second language in early childhood end up closer to native-like command than people who begin as adults, and the difference is clearest in pronunciation: a late learner who has spoken a language fluently for decades will often still carry an accent that a child immigrant lost within a few years. What the evidence supports, however, is a slope rather than a window. The image of a door that slams shut at a fixed age is the part of the popular picture least able to survive scrutiny.

Several things complicate the story that age alone is at work. Children and adults who move to a new country do not learn under the same conditions. The child is enrolled in school, surrounded for hours each day by speakers of the new language and given every incentive to sound like them; the adult often works among speakers of her first language, uses the new one for limited purposes and has an identity already settled in the old. When late learners are compared with early ones, these differences in the quantity and character of exposure travel along with age, and it is hard to tell how much of the outcome each explains. Where adults are immersed in the way children are, some reach levels that the stricter versions of the window theory say should be out of reach.

It also matters what is being measured. Accent appears most sensitive to the age of first exposure, and some aspects of grammar, such as fine judgements about word endings, seem sensitive too. Vocabulary, by contrast, goes on growing throughout life in a first language and a second alike, and adults often learn the early stages of a new language faster than young children do, because they bring better memory strategies and a developed grasp of how languages work. A single critical period for language as a whole therefore looks less plausible than a set of different sensitivities, declining at different rates for different components.

None of this makes early exposure unimportant, and a parent who can give a child two languages from the start gives something valuable. But the window image has costs of its own. It persuades adults that serious learning is no longer open to them, so that they invest less and expect little, and then treats the resulting modest achievement as confirmation. A more accurate picture, in which age makes some things harder and a few things much harder without closing the door at any fixed point, is less dramatic but more useful.

passage: For a long time economists were embarrassed by a simple question. Water is essential to life and diamonds are not, yet water is cheap and diamonds are dear; how could prices, which were supposed to reflect value, so plainly invert the order of importance? Eighteenth-century writers posed the puzzle as a contrast between value in use and value in exchange, and many concluded that exchange value must therefore have some source other than usefulness. The most influential answer located that source in the costs of production, and above all in labour: diamonds are dear because finding and cutting them takes enormous effort, while water, in most places, merely has to be collected.

The cost theory had obvious merits, since goods that are hard to produce are frequently expensive, but it struggled with cases in which effort and price come apart. A pearl found by chance in an oyster served at dinner fetches no less than one obtained by days of diving, and a wine from a celebrated year commands its price long after the labour that made it has been forgotten. The resolution that eventually prevailed, worked out independently by several writers in the later nineteenth century, abandoned the attempt to attach value to goods as such. What matters, it held, is not the usefulness of water in general but the usefulness of one more unit of it to someone who already has a certain amount. A person with enough water to drink, cook and wash would gain little from an extra bucket, while a person with few diamonds, or none, would prize one more highly. Price tracks this marginal usefulness, not the total.

The resolution is genuine, and its elegance is rightly admired. But it achieved both more than it is usually credited with and less. It achieved more because it moved value from things to situations: the same bucket of water is nearly worthless in a town beside a river and beyond price to a traveller lost in a desert, although nothing about the water has changed. It achieved less because it was never a theory of importance. To say that water is cheap is to say that, where it is plentiful, nobody would give much for one more unit of it; it is not to say that water matters little. The marginal account explains why prices may be low on goods that are indispensable, and in doing so it warns us against reading prices as a ranking of what matters.

That warning is regularly forgotten. Public argument often treats the market price of something as the measure of its contribution, so that an activity commanding high prices is assumed to be more valuable to society than one commanding low ones, and resources that cost nothing, such as clean air, are treated as though they were of no account until they become scarce. The marginal theory does not license this inference; if anything it predicts the error, since it shows that abundance alone can drive a price towards zero whatever the total importance of the good. Abundance, moreover, is not always permanent, and a price set while a resource was plentiful says little about what it will be worth once it is not.

None of this is a case against prices, which remain an unrivalled means of coordinating what millions of people do with information that no single mind possesses. It is a case for remembering what question a price answers. A price tells us what one more unit of something is worth to those at the margin, here and now. It does not tell us what the whole of it is worth, or what it would be worth to people who are not in the market at all, and a society that forgets the difference may discover the value of its cheapest goods only when it is too late to pay for them.

passage: In a handful of democracies, adults who fail to vote without a good excuse are fined a small sum. To many people elsewhere this looks like a contradiction in terms: surely a free citizen is entitled to stay at home. The objection deserves a hearing, but it is less forceful than it first appears. What such laws typically require is attendance, not a vote for anyone in particular. Ballots remain secret, and a citizen who wishes to register indifference or protest can spoil the ballot paper or leave it blank. The duty imposed is closer to that of serving on a jury or completing a census form than to an order about what to believe. A subtler version of the objection holds that deliberate abstention is itself a political statement, a refusal to lend legitimacy to a contest one regards as empty. Yet a citizen who feels this way loses very little under compulsion, since the blank ballot preserves the statement and arguably sharpens it: a deliberately empty ballot can be counted, whereas a deliberate absence is indistinguishable from the absences of those who merely forgot.

The more interesting question is what compulsion actually changes. Where voting is voluntary, turnout is usually lowest among the young, the poor and the recently arrived, so the electorate that politicians court is older and wealthier than the population as a whole. Campaigns respond rationally to this. A large share of their effort goes into persuading their own likely supporters to turn up, and one of the cheapest ways to do that is to make those supporters angry or afraid about the other side. When almost everyone votes, that strategy loses much of its point. There is little to be gained by stirring up people who will vote anyway, and the votes worth competing for belong to citizens who have not yet made up their minds.

Supporters of compulsion sometimes go further and claim that it produces wiser decisions. Here caution is needed. Being required to attend a polling station does not make anyone better informed, and a citizen who resents the obligation may simply mark the first name on the list. Compulsion enlarges the electorate; it does not educate it. Its real contribution is quieter. It shifts the incentives of those who seek votes, away from rousing the faithful and towards addressing the undecided, and it allows the result to claim to speak for nearly everyone rather than for those who happened to feel strongly enough to come out. That is a modest achievement, but in an age of angry campaigning it is not a small one.

passage: Few moral injunctions are now repeated with more confidence than the injunction to remember. After a civil war, a dictatorship or a period of communal violence, it is taken almost for granted that the truth must be told, the dead named and the guilty identified, and that a society which declines to do so is building its future on a lie. The case for this view is strong, and nothing that follows is meant to deny it. Those who suffered have a claim to be believed, and a society that teaches its children a false account of its own recent past does them a lasting harm. But the view carries an assumption that deserves examination: that remembering, in public and in detail, is always what allows former enemies to go on living side by side.

The historical record is less obliging than the injunction. A number of societies, ancient and modern, have made peace by agreeing, in one form or another, not to reopen the wrongs of the conflict just ended. Such agreements are often described as attempts at forgetting, but the description is misleading. No decree can make people forget what they suffered or what they did, and none of these arrangements tried to. What they established was something narrower: a rule about the public use of the past. Past crimes would not be prosecuted, or not beyond a certain point; old grievances would not be made the basis of political campaigns; the question of who had done what to whom would, for a time, be kept out of the courts and the assemblies, even as it continued to be remembered in kitchens and graveyards.

Whether such a rule is wise seems to depend less on the principle involved than on timing. In the first years after a conflict, when the losing side still has the means to fight and the institutions of the new order are fragile, a full public reckoning may reopen the war it is meant to close, and the people most likely to pay for that are the ones a reckoning was supposed to vindicate. A generation later, the balance may look quite different. The armed men have grown old, the institutions have settled, and the children of those who suffered may reasonably ask why the silence that once protected the peace should still protect those who did the harm.

For the costs of silence do not fall evenly. The perpetrator who is spared prosecution gains something definite; the victim who is asked not to speak of what was done gives something up, and is often asked to do so by people who lost far less. A peace that rests indefinitely on such an asymmetry is unlikely to remain a peace in any full sense. It may endure as an arrangement while decaying as a settlement, leaving resentments that later politicians find all too easy to exploit.

The upshot is that agreed silence should be judged neither as a betrayal of memory nor as a model of wisdom, but as a provisional arrangement whose legitimacy depends on what happens to it later. A silence that a society chooses, and later chooses to break, may have served both peace and justice in their turn. The worst outcome is not silence as such but a silence that becomes permanent by default, that no one ever decides to keep, and that is mistaken, by those who benefit from it, for a consensus that was never actually reached.
